full_query:
A 43-year-old man presents to the emergency department with bright red blood in his stool this morning. He noticed this yesterday as well, but it was much scanter. The patient is otherwise healthy. He was celebrating his birthday last night and admits having "too much to drink" and vomited profusely overnight. He currently feels well and is not nauseous. He has no other significant medical history and does not take any medications. His temperature is 99.2°F (37.3°C), blood pressure is 110/75 mmHg, pulse is 82/min, respirations are 16/min, and oxygen saturation is 100% on room air. Physical exam reveals a nontender abdomen with normal bowel sounds. Rectal exam reveals grossly bloody stool. Laboratory studies are ordered as shown below.

Hemoglobin: 12 g/dL
Hematocrit: 36%
Leukocyte count: 5,500/mm^3 with normal differential
Platelet count: 179,000/mm^3

Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms? (A) Erosion into a gastric vessel (B) Inflammation and infection of colonic outpouching (C) Malignancy (D) Submucosal esophageal tear (E) Vascular malformation

shared_context.medical_history: otherwise healthy; heavy alcohol consumption and profuse vomiting overnight
shared_context.exam_findings: nontender abdomen, normal bowel sounds, grossly bloody stool on rectal exam

sentences: To determine the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms, we need to evaluate his clinical presentation and laboratory findings step-by-step
Clinical Presentation: The patient has bright red blood in his stool, which began yesterday and was more pronounced today
Bright red blood per rectum (hematochezia) often indicates bleeding from the lower gastrointestinal (GI) tract, such as the colon, rectum, or anus
However, it can occasionally be caused by massive upper GI bleeding
History: The patient mentioned heavy alcohol consumption and vomiting profusely overnight
This is a critical point as it suggests a possible upper GI etiology
Temperature: 99.2°F (37.3°C) - within normal range
Blood pressure: 110/75 mmHg - normal
Pulse: 82/min - normal
Respirations: 16/min - normal
Oxygen saturation: 100% on room air - normal
Physical exam: nontender abdomen, normal bowel sounds, and grossly bloody stool on rectal exam
Hemoglobin: 12 g/dL (normal range: 13.8 to 17.2 g/dL for men) - slightly low
Hematocrit: 36% (normal range: 41% to 50% for men) - slightly low
Leukocyte count: 5,500/mm^3 with normal differential - normal
Platelet count: 179,000/mm^3 - normal
Erosion into a gastric vessel (A): This would typically present with melena (black, tarry stools) or hematemesis (vomiting blood) rather than bright red blood per rectum
Inflammation and infection of colonic outpouching (B): This refers to diverticulitis, which usually presents with left lower quadrant pain, fever, and leukocytosis
The patient's clinical picture does not match this scenario
Malignancy (C): Colorectal cancer can present with rectal bleeding, but the acute onset associated with vomiting suggests a more acute cause
Submucosal esophageal tear (D): Known as a Mallory-Weiss tear, this condition is commonly associated with forceful vomiting leading to upper GI bleeding
This fits the patient's history of heavy alcohol use and vomiting
Vascular malformation (E): Such as angiodysplasia, can cause lower GI bleeding but is less likely given the acute presentation and recent vomiting episode

Based on the patient's history of heavy alcohol consumption and vomiting, combined with the presence of bright red blood per rectum and a slight decrease in hemoglobin and hematocrit, the most likely diagnosis is a Mallory-Weiss tear (D)
